# Between Sleeps

In the winter of 1695, somewhere in the English countryside, a farmer woke in the dark. This was not insomnia. He had gone to bed a few hours after sundown, when the fire had burned down to a red insistence in the grate, and he had slept deeply. Now he was awake again — not groggily, not with the ragged panic of the modern 3 a.m. mind, but cleanly, the way you wake when a first sleep has done its work. He thought about the fields, or a debt, or a verse of scripture. Perhaps he reached over and woke his wife. Perhaps they talked, quietly, about the kind of things people will only say in the dark. In a while he would sleep again, and that second sleep had a name of its own, and neither sleep was considered the strange one.

This happened every night, to nearly everyone, and within a few generations it had almost entirely vanished from the world.

The historian Roger Ekirch spent years in the archives before he understood what he was looking at. Again and again, in diaries, court records, ballads, medical texts, and prayer books from the pre-industrial world, he found references to a way of sleeping that no one had thought to mention in a long time: sleep in two parts. The Italians said *primo sonno*. The French said *premier sommeil*. In English it was "first sleep" and "second sleep," and the hour or two of quiet wakefulness between them — the distinctive, hovering consciousness we now experience mainly as a symptom — was called the watch, or, in French, *dorveille*, a word that means both sleeping and waking at once.

The documents are full of it. A fifteenth-century prayer book includes devotions to be said "in the morning, between the first sleep and the second." A French peasant testifying in 1699 explains that the crime occurred before he "had had his first sleep." People in the watch prayed. They smoked. They got up and checked the livestock, or did a little quiet work by the banked fire. In villages, some of them visited neighbors; the night, before it was conquered, had a social geography we would now find alarming — people moving between houses under a sky genuinely black, a darkness that no longer exists over most of the inhabited world.

And then the light came.

First there were more candles, then oil lamps, then gas, then electricity, each generation pushing the evening further back and compressing the night. Sleep, which had been a wide landscape with a valley in the middle, began to close like a book. By the 1920s, when electric light was finally reaching ordinary homes in Europe and America, the consolidated eight-hour block had become the standard, and the old two-part rhythm — no longer practiced, no longer permitted by the lit evening — started to look like a disorder. Doctors began seeing patients who woke in the middle of the night and couldn't get back down, and they named it: middle-of-the-night insomnia, a pathology. It may simply have been the watch, knocking on a door that had been painted over.

I think about this more than is probably reasonable, because it seems to me one of the cleanest examples we have of something enormous and quiet: the way a form of consciousness can go extinct. Not a species, not even a language, but a room in the mind. For thousands of years, human beings passed every night through a state that was neither sleeping nor being awake in the daylight sense — a state with its own name, its own prayers, its own uses. People brought their dreams out into it while the dreams were still wet. They had sex in it. They did the interior work that daylight, with its tasks and other people, does not permit. The watch was built into the architecture of the night, and when we rebuilt the night we didn't relocate the room; we walled it up.

None of this is an argument for going back. I like electric light. I like that the night is no longer the property of the desperate and the criminal; I like being able to read at midnight without setting the house on fire. Pre-industrial night was cold, dangerous, and often frightened. The dark was a real darkness, full of things the daylight kept offstage. The people lying awake in the watch were not all having mellow, lantern-lit philosophical hours. Some were terrified. Some were grieving. Some were listening for thieves. Nostalgia for the old night is mostly nostalgia for a painting of it.

But there is a difference between not wanting to return somewhere and refusing to notice what was lost on the way out. What went missing wasn't just a sleep schedule. It was a sanctioned interval of liminality — a time when being awake in the small hours was not a failure of sleep but a different country with its own customs. We still visit that country. Nearly everyone does. The 3 a.m. waking is among the most common sleep complaints in the world, and anyone who has lain there knows its particular quality: not day-thought, not dream, a third thing, raw and unguarded, in which the mind turns over material it would never permit itself at noon. We treat this as a malfunction. We lie there criticizing ourselves for it, which is to say we meet the old watch with the new night's values, and so we spoil even that.

I don't know what to do with this knowledge, exactly. Sometimes, when I wake at three, I try to give the hour its old name, to sit up in the dark and let it be what it used to be — to not reach for the phone, whose glow is the last and brightest link in the chain that began with the first candle. It rarely works. The phone is right there, and the day is already leaking in at the edges of the hour: emails, headlines, the whole electric continent. The watch doesn't open easily anymore. It opens, when it opens, onto the same lit room we never leave.

Still, I like knowing it was there. I like knowing that for most of human history, when a person woke at two in the morning and stared at the dark, they were not failing. They were keeping an appointment the whole species kept, in the space between two sleeps, in a darkness we have since abolished, in a state of mind we no longer have a word for and so no longer know how to enter — except by accident, at three a.m., when it enters us.

**Between Sleeps**

In the winter of 1695, somewhere in the English countryside, a farmer woke in the dark. This was not insomnia. He had gone to bed a few hours after sundown, when the fire had burned down to a red insistence in the grate, and he had slept deeply. Now he was awake again — not groggily, not with the ragged panic of the modern 3 a.m. mind, but cleanly, the way you wake when a first sleep has done its work. He lay still for a while. He thought about the fields, or a debt, or a verse of scripture. Perhaps he reached over and woke his wife. Perhaps they talked, quietly, about the kind of things people will only say in the dark. In a while he would sleep again, and that second sleep had a name of its own, and neither sleep was considered the strange one.

This happened every night, to nearly everyone, and within a few generations it had almost entirely vanished from the world.

The historian Roger Ekirch spent fifteen years in the archives before he understood what he was looking at. Again and again, in diaries, court records, ballads, medical texts, and prayer books from the pre-industrial world, he found references to a mode of sleep that no one had thought to mention in a long time: sleep in two parts. The Italians said primo sonno. The French said premier sommeil. In English it was "first sleep" and "second sleep," and the hour or two of quiet wakefulness between them — the distinctive, hovering consciousness that we now experience mainly as a symptom — was called the watch, or, in French, dorveille, a lovely word that means both sleep and waking at once.

The documents are full of it. A fifteenth-century prayer book includes devotions to be said "in the morning, between the first sleep and the second." A French peasant in a 1699 court case testifies that he "had not yet had his first sleep" when the crime occurred._ballads, letters, a seventeenth-century physician noting that his patients' dreams came most truly "after the first sleep" — which happens to be when modern sleep researchers find the most vivid dreams occur, if you happen to sleep in one unbroken stretch and wake at the right moment. People in the watch prayed. They smoked. They got up and checked the livestock, or did a little quiet work by the banked fire. In villages, some of them visited neighbors; the night, before it was conquered, had a social geography we would now find alarming — people moving between houses under a sky genuinely black, the kind of darkness that no longer exists over most of the inhabited world.

And then the light came.

It didn't arrive all at once. First there were more candles, then oil lamps, then gas, then electricity, each generation pushing the evening further back and compressing the night. Sleep, which had been a wide landscape with a valley in the middle, began to close like a book. By the 1920s, when electric light was finally reaching ordinary homes in Europe and America, the consolidated eight-hour block was becoming the standard, and the old two-part rhythm — no longer practiced, no longer permitted by the lit evening — started to look like a disorder. Doctors began to see patients who woke in the middle of the night and couldn't get back down, and they named it insomnia, middle-of-the-night insomnia, a pathology. It may simply have been the watch, knocking on a door that had been painted over.

I think about this more than is probably reasonable, because it seems to me one of the cleanest examples we have of something enormous and quiet: the way a form of consciousness can go extinct. Not a species, not a language even, but a room in the mind. For thousands of years, human beings passed every night through a state that was neither sleeping nor being awake in the daylight sense — a state with its own name, its own prayers, its own uses. People brought their dreams out into it while the dreams were still wet. They had sex in it. They did the interior work that daylight, with its tasks and other people, doesn't permit. The watch was built into the architecture of the night, and when we rebuilt the night we didn't relocate the room; we walled it up.

None of this is an argument for going back. I like electric light. I like that the night is no longer the property of the desperate and the criminal; I like being able to read at midnight without setting the house on fire. Ekirch himself is careful about this. Pre-industrial night was cold, dangerous, and often frightened. The dark was a real darkness, full of things the daylight kept offstage. The people lying awake in the watch were not all having mellow, lantern-lit philosophical hours. Some were terrified. Some were grieving. Some were listening for thieves. Nostalgia for the old night is mostly nostalgia for a painting of it.

But there is a difference between not wanting to return somewhere and refusing to notice what was lost on the way out. What went missing wasn't just a sleep schedule. It was a sanctioned interval of liminality — a time when being awake in the small hours was not a failure of sleep but a different country with its own customs. We still visit that country. Nearly everyone does. The 3 a.m. waking is among the most common sleep complaints in the world, and anyone who has lain there knows its particular quality: not day-thought, not dream, a third thing, raw and unguarded, in which the mind turns over material it would never permit itself at noon. We treat this as a malfunction. We lie there criticizing ourselves for it, which is to say we meet the old watch with the new night's values, and so we spoil even that.

I don't know what to do with this knowledge, exactly. Sometimes, when I wake at three, I try to give it the old name, to sit up in the dark and let the hour be what it used to be — to not reach for the phone, whose light is the last and brightest link in that chain that began with the first candle. It rarely works. The phone is right there, and the day is already leaking in at the edges of the hour, emails, headlines, the whole electric continent. The watch doesn't open easily anymore; it opens, when it opens, onto the same lit room we never leave.

Still, I like knowing it was there. I like knowing that for most of human history, when a person woke at two in the morning and stared at the dark, they were not failing. They were keeping an appointment their whole species kept, in the space between two sleeps, in a darkness we have since abolished, in a state of mind we no longer have a word for and so no longer know how to enter — except by accident, at three a.m., when it enters us.
